newsitem.title: USA: Dlr settles above 122 yen in US after fresh high.
newsitem.headline: Dlr settles above 122 yen in US after fresh high.

text.p: The dollar ended broadly higher in U.S. trade on Wednesday after surging to another near four-year high against the yen in overseas trade.
Dealers attributed the gains to a growing sense in the market that Japan is willing to tolerate persistent weakness in its currency.

Remarks from Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka suggested Japan is unlikely to actively defend the yen soon, and another day of sharp gains in Japanese stocks both contributed to the perception that Japan has no urgent desire or need to reverse yen weakness, they said.

Against the mark, the dollar rebounded from an overseas drop to end modestly stronger. Dollar/mark had sold off initially in European trade after Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said the dollar's rise against the mark was nearing an end.
The dollar ended the day at 122.15/20 yen, up from 121.55/65 at the open. It touched a peak of 122.75 yen, its highest level since early February of 1993, in Asian trade.
The dollar closed at 1.6435/45 marks, above its opening level of 1.6395/00.
The dollar's gains against the yen were kept in check earlier in the week by fears that Japan's central bank would intervene to stem the yen's fall.

But on Wednesday, Mitsuzuka said that "calling for stable currencies could lead to stability itself," a sign to many in the market that Japan is likely to continue to use rhetoric rather than active currency intervention to curb excessive yen weakness.
The pressure on Japan to defend the yen was also alleviated by more gains in Japanese stocks, traders said.

The Nikkei average of 225 leading Japanese shares, which has slumped badly in recent months, prompting concerns about weakness in the yen, jumped over 530 points on Wednesday after rising some 461 points on Tuesday.

"As the domestic Japanese markets stabilize, I think the perception is that there will be less pressure on the Japanese to defend the yen," said John Nelson, foreign exchange trading manager at ABN-AMRO Bank in Chicago.
Against the mark, dip-buying lifted the dollar off early lows, brought about by remarks from Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer.
The German central bank chief said on Wednesday that he expected the "normalization" of the mark's exchange rate against the dollar to end soon, prompting an early flood of dollar sales.

"Tietmeyer's comments were a key development," said Marc Chandler, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "People used them as an excuse to sell the dollar against the mark and other European currencies."
But Chandler said dollar/mark bounced up from technical support around 1.6350 and climbed steadily in U.S. trade based on favorable dollar fundamentals.
"The prospect of strong U.S. economic data contrasted with weak European and Asian data continue to favor the dollar," said Chandler.

Elsewhere, the dollar ended stronger at 1.4260/70 Swiss francs against 1.4190/00 at the open, after the chairman of the Swiss central bank said that the weakening franc was helping the struggling Swiss economy.
Sterling ended modestly weaker at $1.6199/04 versus $1.6205/15 at the open. The dollar advanced to Canadian $1.3450/55 against C$1.3433/38.
The Australian dollar firmed to $0.7706/11 after opening at $0.7683/88.
